meta.title: Who really said "Do you feel lucky, punk?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Nobody. Harry Callahan says “You’ve got to ask yourself one question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’ Well, do ya, punk?” in Dirty Harry (1971). The pronoun is the point.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do you feel lucky, punk?'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is never spoken. Dirty Harry (1971) says “Do I feel lucky?” — Harry hands the robber the question. Verified against AFI and Wikiquote.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “Do I feel lucky?”

answer.sourceLine: Inspector Harry Callahan never says “Do you feel lucky, punk?” in Dirty Harry (1971). What he says is “You’ve got to ask yourself one question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’ Well, do ya, punk?” — the wording the American Film Institute ranked 51st among the greatest movie quotes ↗. The film is the right source; only the words drifted.
answer.confidenceText: The wording is wrong, but the film and its writers are right — the drift is in how the line is repeated, not in who made it.

source.heading: The actual line, in context

docMeta.dd: Insp. Harry Callahan (Clint Eastwood) — a fictional character — to a wounded bank robber (Albert Popwell); repeated at the film’s close to the Scorpio killer (Andy Robinson)
Screenplay: Harry Julian Fink, R. M. Fink and Dean Riesner. Story: Harry Julian Fink and R. M. Fink. Uncredited draft work by John Milius and Terrence Malick.
Warner Bros., Inc. / The Malpaso Company · directed by Don Siegel · original screenplay, working title Dead Right

source.excerpt: I know what you’re thinking: ‘Did he fire six shots or only five?’ Well, to tell you the truth, in all this excitement, I’ve kinda lost track myself. But being this is a .44 Magnum, the most powerful handgun in the world, and would blow your head clean off… You’ve got to ask yourself one question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’ Well, do ya, punk?
trail: The film’s own catalog record. The AFI Catalog entry for Dirty Harry ↗ quotes the speech “ending with the words ‘You’ve got to ask yourself one question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’ Well do ya, punk?’”, notes it became an iconic catchphrase after release, and records that the same speech is repeated at the end of the film.

The AFI’s canonical list. Entry No. 51 of 100 Years…100 Movie Quotes ↗ reproduces the full sentence with the inner “Do I feel lucky?” intact — and lists the writers as Harry Julian Fink, R. M. Fink and Dean Riesner.

Named as a misquote by the specialists. Wikiquote’s “Misattributed” section ↗ lists “Do you feel lucky, punk?” explicitly and states that the line actually said in the film is the longer one. The Telegraph’s 2014 “Ten film quotes we all get wrong” ↗ makes it their No. 2, observing the misquote “gets across Clint Eastwood’s sentiment perfectly while taking a fifth of the time”.

Origination: the film really is the source. Unlike many famous screen lines, this one was not borrowed from a novel or play. The AFI Catalog lists no source-work credit and records the working title as Dead Right — an original spec script by the Finks, later rewritten by Dean Riesner, with uncredited drafts by John Milius and Terrence Malick ↗. The 1971 Philip Rock novelisation derives from the film, not the reverse.
source.excerptNote: The bolded sentence is the portion the AFI ranked 51st in 100 Years…100 Movie Quotes. AFI renders the last beat “do ya”; some transcriptions, including Wikiquote’s own misattribution note, write “do you” — a contraction judgement, not a factual dispute. What no transcription supports is “Do you feel lucky, punk?”

source.rightsNote: Dirty Harry was released 21–22 December 1971, four decades past the 1930 US public-domain cutoff, and remains firmly in copyright. The AFI Catalog records the copyright claimant as Warner Bros., Inc. & The Malpaso Company, registered 22 December 1971 (LP41628) ↗. Screen writing is work-for-hire, so the rights sit with the studio and production company — not with Fink, Fink or Riesner personally, and not with Clint Eastwood as performer. The line is quoted here in brief for identification and fact-checking.

author.kicker: The writers of the real line
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Credited screenwriters · Dirty Harry (1971), Warner Bros. / The Malpaso Company
author.bio: Harry Julian Fink and his wife Rita M. Fink (credited as R. M. Fink) wrote the original spec script — working title Dead Right — that became Dirty Harry; the AFI Catalog ↗ credits them with both the screenplay and the story, alongside Dean Riesner, who rewrote the script for Clint Eastwood and Don Siegel. The screen credit is shared three ways and quotle.info does not split it further: John Milius and Terrence Malick also worked on uncredited drafts ↗, and a widely repeated claim that Milius personally wrote the “Do I feel lucky?” speech is not supported by any source we could verify — in his own 1976 Film Comment interview Milius described his contribution as “a lot of guns” and Harry’s attitude, not this speech. What is certain is the author class: the line belongs to the writers, not to the character and not to the actor.

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong here
misattribution.intro: No one is falsely credited on this one. The film is real, the writers are real, and the line is very nearly real — the error is entirely in the wording, and it is the kind of error that reverses the meaning rather than merely trimming it. Here is what the popular version gets wrong, and one adjacent mix-up worth clearing up.

items.why: The film’s pronoun is I, not you. Harry quotes the question the robber must ask himself — “you’ve got to ask yourself one question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’” — so the words “Do I feel lucky” are the robber’s line, ventriloquised. AFI’s official list preserves the quotation-within-a-quotation ↗. The popular version deletes the frame and the inner pronoun with it.

“Punk” is not attached to the lucky question. It lands in a separate sentence after it — “Well, do ya, punk?” — and in the film’s closing confrontation with Scorpio the two halves are split across a pause while Scorpio reaches for his gun ↗. The misquote welds them into a single glib taunt.

Eastwood delivered the line and produced the film, but the writing credit is Harry Julian Fink, R. M. Fink and Dean Riesner, per the AFI Catalog’s credits ↗. A screen line’s author is its writer. Harry Callahan, being fictional, cannot be its author at all.

Frequently bolted onto Dirty Harry in the same breath as this line, but Harry does not say it in the 1971 film. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed to this film ↗; he first says it in Sudden Impact (1983).

misattribution.truthLine: The film originated the line and the credited writers wrote it — but the sentence the public repeats was never spoken. The real one is “You’ve got to ask yourself one question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’ Well do ya, punk?” ↗

context.heading: Why the real line is better than the misquote
lead: The popular version does not just shorten the line — it inverts it. In the film, Harry is not asking the robber whether he feels lucky. He is telling the man what question the man must now ask himself: “Do I feel lucky?” is quoted speech, placed in the robber’s own mouth. Harry then steps back out of it for the taunt: “Well, do ya, punk?” The gun is pointed, the arithmetic is unresolved, and the decision has been handed to the man on the ground. Flattening it to “Do you feel lucky, punk?” puts the question back in Harry’s mouth and throws away the whole manoeuvre.

The speech occurs twice. The famous delivery is in the opening bank-robbery sequence — a scene the AFI Catalog notes was unrelated to the main storyline ↗ and was the one sequence not shot on location in San Francisco — addressed to a wounded robber played by Albert Popwell, who answers “I gots to know…” and gets an empty chamber. Harry repeats the speech at the film’s close to the Scorpio killer, who reaches for his gun and does not get an empty chamber.
context.detailsSummary: A note on “do ya” versus “do you”
detailsBody: Sources differ on the final two beats. The AFI’s official quote list and the AFI Catalog both render it “Well, do ya, punk?”, as does Wikiquote’s scene transcript. Wikiquote’s own “Misattributed” note and Wikipedia’s plot summary instead write “Well, do you, punk?” — an inconsistency internal to those pages.

We give “do ya” because it is what the two AFI records say and what the delivery sounds like, but this is a transcription judgement about a contraction, not a factual dispute. Either way, the popular “Do you feel lucky, punk?” is wrong for a different and larger reason: the pronoun on feel lucky is I, not you.
context.pull: “Do I feel lucky?” is the robber’s question, not Harry’s. The misquote steals it back.
